standards.why: Sonner's API gives the toast container an ARIA label and a keyboard shortcut that focuses the toaster area, and with dismissible: false the user cannot dismiss the toast; keeping these defaults as the house default is a reading of the API reference [inferred].

standards.title: Never trap the user in an overlay
standards.rule: Give every screen and overlay a way out: keep drawers dismissible by outside click, Escape and drag by default, and if one must be non-dismissible, give it an explicit close control such as Drawer.Close [inferred].
standards.why: Every screen should answer 'How do I get out?'; never trap the user. A non-dismissible Vaul drawer blocks outside click, Escape and drag, and the docs' own demo can then only be closed by refreshing the page; pairing it with Vaul's Close part ('the button that closes the drawer') is our connection [inferred]. (Vaul is good-to-have and unmaintained per its README, recorded in learn/sources.json on 2026-09-24.)

standards.title: Controlled drawers still react to Escape
standards.rule: When a Vaul drawer is controlled with the open prop, also pass onOpenChange so the app reacts to Escape and outside clicks.
standards.why: onOpenChange is called when the open state changes, which the docs call useful for reacting to esc/outside clicks when the drawer is controlled. (Vaul is good-to-have and unmaintained per its README, recorded in learn/sources.json on 2026-09-24.)

standards.title: Cover the inert page behind a drawer
standards.rule: While a modal drawer or sheet is open, render its overlay so a layer covers the inert rest of the view.
standards.why: Vaul's Overlay is the layer that covers the inert portion of the view when the drawer is open, and a modal task pairs its surface with a dimming scrim. (Vaul is good-to-have and unmaintained per its README, recorded in learn/sources.json on 2026-09-24.)

standards.title: Never disable pinch zoom
standards.rule: Never set user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1 in the viewport meta tag; when the page zooms into an input, fix the input's font size (16px at the minimum) instead.
standards.why: user-scalable=no and maximum-scale=1 are accessibility failures; the zoom they are used to stop comes from iOS Safari zooming into inputs under 16px, so the font size is the thing to fix.

review.message: Disabling zoom is an accessibility failure; remove it and set inputs to at least 16px so iOS does not zoom into them.

standards.title: Mount one Toaster at the root
standards.rule: Mount exactly one <Toaster /> once, as close to the app root as possible (in Next.js, layout.tsx), and never render it per page, conditionally, or in both a layout and a page.
standards.why: A second mounted Toaster duplicates every toast, and an unmounted one means toasts never appear.

standards.title: Keep the Toaster outside stacking contexts
standards.rule: Mount the Toaster at the document root, outside any dialog or portal container and outside any ancestor with transform, filter or overflow.
standards.why: Such an ancestor creates a stacking context, or the overlay out-z-indexes the toaster, so toasts sit behind a modal or get clipped.

standards.title: Call toast() only from client code
standards.rule: Call toast() only from client code (event handlers, effects, callbacks); in a server action, return the result and call toast() in the client code that receives it.
standards.why: toast() is a plain function that does nothing on the server.

standards.title: Fire toasts from handlers or stable ids
standards.rule: Fire toasts from event handlers; when a toast must fire from an effect, pass a stable id so a repeated call updates the toast instead of duplicating it.
standards.why: React StrictMode's dev double-invoke runs effects twice; a stable id makes the second call update rather than duplicate.

standards.title: Web toast enter: 400ms ease from below
standards.rule: On the web, enter a toast from opacity: 0 and transform: translateY(100%) to its settled position with transition: opacity 400ms ease, transform 400ms ease, using @starting-style (or a mounted flag set in useEffect where @starting-style is unavailable).
standards.why: A toast that suddenly appears feels off; Sonner uses ease rather than ease-out and runs slightly slower than typical UI because its motion is tuned to the component's personality.

engine.note: new token for the toast enter/exit transition
new token for CSS `ease`; the cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1) equivalence comes from the CSS spec, not the source [inferred]

standards.title: React Native toasts: 300ms in, 250ms out
standards.rule: In React Native, enter toasts with FadeInDown.duration(300).easing(EASE_OUT), exit with FadeOutDown.duration(250).easing(EASE_OUT), keep them within the 300ms cap, and define both builders at module scope.
standards.why: A toast is uninvited, so it should be quicker and quieter than motion the user asked for; the user has finished reading, so the exit runs about 20% faster than the entry.

standards.title: Stack toasts with lift and depth
standards.rule: In the collapsed stack, position toasts absolutely, lift each toast behind the front one by the gap times its index, and scale it down by 0.05 per index; apply this only to non-front toasts while the stack is collapsed.
standards.why: Absolute positioning simplifies the stacking, and scaling the toasts behind down creates a sense of depth.

values.examples: Y(0) scale(1); Y(-14px) scale(0.95); Y(-28px) scale(0.9)

standards.title: Stacked toasts share the front height
standards.rule: While toasts are stacked, give every toast the height of the toast in front.
standards.why: Toasts with different heights otherwise do not stick out evenly behind the front toast.

standards.title: Expand the toast stack on hover
standards.rule: Keep the toast stack collapsed and expand it while the pointer hovers the toast area (expand: false by default); when expanded, offset each toast by its index times the gap plus the heights of the toasts before it, with a gap of 14.
standards.why: Stacked mode hides older toasts and hovering reveals them; toasts can differ in height, so each expanded offset adds the real heights above it.

engine.note: new token; Sonner documents gap as the number 14 without a unit, so px is [inferred]

standards.title: Fill gaps between toasts for hover
standards.rule: Fill the gaps between expanded toasts with an :after pseudo-element so the hover state holds while the pointer crosses a gap.
standards.why: The gaps belong to no toast, so hovering them would make the toasts lose their hover state (and collapse).

standards.title: Show at most three toasts
standards.rule: Show at most 3 toasts at once by default (visibleToasts: 3).
standards.why: 3 is Sonner's documented default number of visible toasts.

engine.note: New token, created in every export from this mapping's number type (engine.py std_token_types).

standards.title: Auto-dismiss toasts after 4 seconds, except action toasts
standards.rule: Auto-close toasts after 4000ms by default, except a toast that carries an action button (Undo, Retry): it stays until the person acts on it or dismisses it (Sonner: duration: Infinity on that toast() call).
standards.why: 4000ms is Sonner's default duration: by default the toast disappears after 4 seconds unless you hover over it. A toast with an action is the exception: closing it on a timer puts a time limit on the action, and the accessibility floors outrank every house standard (docs/KNOWLEDGE.md section 2; WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable), so it persists; this agrees with DC-L08-18 and the Q-form-04 option inline-banner [inferred: no source states the exception].

values.action-toast: no auto-close: duration: Infinity on that toast() call, until the person acts or dismisses it [inferred]

engine.note: new token for the toast auto-dismiss time

standards.title: Pause the toast timer on hover
standards.rule: Pause the auto-dismiss timer while the pointer hovers the toasts.
standards.why: The toast disappears after 4 seconds unless you hover over it, so a person reading it keeps it.

standards.title: Pause toast timers in a hidden tab
standards.rule: Pause the auto-dismiss timer while the document is hidden (document.hidden and the visibilitychange event).
standards.why: A toast fired while the person is on another tab would otherwise time out unseen; an inactive tab should freeze its toasts.

standards.title: Swipe toasts away along their position
standards.rule: Let people swipe or drag toasts and drawers away, on touch devices and on desktop; for toasts the allowed swipe directions follow the toaster position, and swipeDirections is overridden only when they must differ.
standards.why: People are used to swiping notifications away on their devices, and Sonner derives the swipe directions from the position.

standards.title: Pick the toast call by need
standards.rule: Pick the toast() call by what the message needs: toast('Title') with { description } for plain messages, toast.success/error/info/warning for status, toast.promise for work tied to one promise, toast.loading plus an update by id when you manage the states yourself, { action } / { cancel } for buttons, and toast.custom for headless JSX.
standards.why: Typed calls carry the matching icon, the promise toast starts loading and switches to success or error on its own, and the action button closes the toast unless onClick calls event.preventDefault().

values.action: { action: { label, onClick } }; event.preventDefault() keeps it open; cancel is the secondary button

standards.title: Promise toasts need a settling promise
standards.rule: Pass toast.promise a promise, or a function returning one, that actually resolves or rejects.
standards.why: Otherwise the loading toast waits forever and never closes.

standards.title: Update a toast by its id
standards.rule: To change a toast already on screen, keep the id toast() returns and call toast() (or a typed call such as toast.success) again with that id, passing only the props that change, instead of adding a new toast.
standards.why: Calling toast() with the same id updates the existing toast, only the props you pass change, and a typed call switches its type.

standards.title: Toasts follow the app theme
standards.rule: In an app with a dark theme, set the Toaster theme to 'system' or pass the theme provider's resolved theme (for example <Toaster theme={resolvedTheme} /> from next-themes).
standards.why: theme defaults to 'light' and does not track the OS, so dark mode is otherwise ignored.

standards.title: Rich colors and invert from defaults
standards.rule: Start toast styling from Sonner's defaults: add richColors on the Toaster when success and error must read green and red, and use invert only to flip toasts against the theme.
standards.why: Success and error toasts are gray by default; richColors and invert are the first rung of the styling ladder.

standards.title: Headless toast for the design system
standards.rule: Build the design system's toast headless with toast.custom() and your own JSX, wrapped in your own toast() function. Climb the styling ladder (defaults, inline style, classNames, headless) only as far as a change needs: the middle rungs suit a few small changes, and a design-system toast should not linger there.
standards.why: Headless keeps Sonner's positioning, stacking and swipe while giving full control, and it is the recommended approach because people usually either use the defaults or go fully custom; styling parts with classes gets messy quickly and is a good compromise only for a few changes.

values.avoid: unstyled: true (a halfway house; headless gives more control for the same effort)

standards.title: Toast classNames need !important
standards.rule: When styling toast parts through toastOptions.classNames (toast, title, description, actionButton, cancelButton, closeButton), mark every class !important (Tailwind: the ! prefix) unless the toast is unstyled, and go headless once more than a few classes need it.
standards.why: Sonner's injected styles win the cascade, so classes without !important have no effect.

values.parts: toast, title, description, actionButton, cancelButton, closeButton

standards.title: Set toast defaults on the Toaster
standards.rule: Put app-wide toast options in the Toaster's toastOptions and override them per toast() call only where needed.
standards.why: Options passed to toast() override the same options set on the Toaster.

standards.title: Target toasts when several toasters exist
standards.rule: When more than one Toaster exists, give each an id and pass toasterId in every toast() call.
standards.why: Without toasterId, every toaster renders the toast.

standards.title: Handle dismiss and auto-close separately
standards.rule: Handle user dismissal in onDismiss and timeouts in onAutoClose, and wire both when code must react to every way a toast closes.
standards.why: onDismiss fires on the close button or a swipe and onAutoClose fires when the toast closes after its duration; there is no single closed callback.

standards.title: Toasts default to bottom-right
standards.rule: Place toasts bottom-right by default, choosing only from top-left, top-center, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-center and bottom-right.
standards.why: bottom-right is Sonner's documented default and these are its six positions; swipe directions follow the position.

values.positions: top-left, top-center, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-center, bottom-right

standards.title: Toaster edge offsets: 32px and 16px
standards.rule: Offset the toaster 32px from the screen edges on desktop and 16px when the screen is narrower than 600px (offset and mobileOffset).
standards.why: These are Sonner's documented default offsets, and mobileOffset applies below a 600px screen width.

engine.note: new token
new token; applies below a 600px screen width

standards.title: Copy Sonner styles into shadow DOM
standards.rule: When rendering Sonner inside shadow DOM, copy the <style> elements in document.head whose text includes [data-sonner-toaster] into the shadow root.
standards.why: Sonner inserts its styles into the document head when the bundle loads, so they are not available inside shadow DOM.

standards.title: Import Sonner styles when they are lost
standards.rule: When toasts render unstyled (Astro, view transitions), import Sonner's stylesheet explicitly in a layout: import 'sonner/dist/styles.css'.
standards.why: Sonner's injected stylesheet was lost.

standards.title: Toast API is a plain function
standards.rule: Expose the design-system toast as a plain toast() function callable from anywhere, with one <Toaster /> mounted once: no hooks and no React context.
standards.why: No hooks, no context, one insert and a function call is one of the two reasons Sonner succeeded; the less friction to adopt, the more people use it (Sonner avoids context with an observer pattern).

standards.title: Prefer drawers over modals on mobile
standards.rule: On mobile, present secondary content in a drawer (bottom sheet) rather than a modal.
standards.why: A drawer gives a more native feel on mobile.

standards.title: Build drawers on an accessible dialog
standards.rule: Build drawers on an accessible dialog primitive (Vaul builds on Radix Dialog) with composable, styleable parts: Root, Trigger, Portal, Overlay, Content, Handle, Title, Description and Close.
standards.why: The dialog primitive makes the drawer accessible and handles focus management, a Radix-like API feels familiar, and not every drawer has to look the same. Vaul itself is unmaintained per its GitHub README (learn/sources.json, checked 2026-09-24); flag that before adding it as a dependency.

values.parts: Drawer.Root, Drawer.Trigger, Drawer.Portal, Drawer.Overlay, Drawer.Content, Drawer.Handle, Drawer.Title, Drawer.Description, Drawer.Close

standards.title: Drawer defaults: modal, bottom, dismissible
standards.rule: Default drawers to modal, opening from the bottom edge, dismissible (outside click, Escape and drag down), draggable from anywhere rather than only the handle, and portalled with an overlay over the inert rest of the view.
standards.why: These are Vaul's Root defaults; dismissible: false blocks all three ways of closing, and the Overlay covers the inert portion of the view. Vaul itself is unmaintained per its GitHub README (learn/sources.json, checked 2026-09-24); flag that before adding it as a dependency.

standards.title: Drawer curve: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)
standards.rule: Animate drawers and sheets that open or close on a timing curve (every web drawer) with the iOS-like drawer curve, defined once as a token: --ease-drawer: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) (React Native: EASE_SHEET = Easing.bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)). Sheets and drawers a finger drives on iOS and Android settle with a spring instead (STD-springs-gestures-08).
standards.why: The curve, from the Ionic Framework, closely matches iOS's sheet; the right easing and duration make a big difference to how the component feels, and built-in CSS easings are too weak.

engine.note: new token (tested: engine.py set creates it in primitives.tokens.json)

standards.title: Drag a drawer only from its scroll top
standards.rule: Let a scrollable drawer be dragged only when its content is scrolled to the top, and block dragging for 100ms after scrolling reaches the top.
standards.why: Being scrollable and draggable at once is tricky; this mirrors native iOS drawers, and fast scrolling can overshoot the top into a drag with enough velocity to close the drawer by accident.

engine.note: New token: time after the content reaches the top during which a drag cannot start.

standards.title: Keep drawer inputs above the keyboard
standards.rule: When an input inside a drawer opens the on-screen keyboard, stop the browser's scroll-into-view and use the Visual Viewport API to size the drawer to the visual viewport and sit it directly above the keyboard (Vaul: repositionInputs, on by default).
standards.why: Otherwise the browser scrolls up and pushes the drawer, potentially hiding important content; sitting above the keyboard keeps the drawer fully scrollable, and the author found this works best despite a slight delay. Vaul itself is unmaintained per its GitHub README (learn/sources.json, checked 2026-09-24); flag that before adding it as a dependency.

standards.title: Fixed-pixel snap points for inputs
standards.rule: Use a fixed-pixel snap point (rather than a fraction of the viewport) when something such as an input must stick out by the same amount on every device.
standards.why: Fixed values make the content stick out evenly on all devices.

values.forms: fraction of the viewport or fixed px

standards.title: React Native: native sheet presentations
standards.rule: In React Native (Expo Router), present a bottom sheet that is its own screen with presentation: 'formSheet' (with detents for a short interruption such as a picker, filter or share), use presentation: 'modal' for a self-contained task the user can abandon, and build a custom drag-to-dismiss sheet only when it must live inside an existing screen.
standards.why: formSheet is a real UISheetPresentationController, free and correct; the navigation table maps each overlay kind to a presentation.

standards.title: React Native: form sheets on both platforms
standards.rule: Design React Native form sheets for both platforms: at most three detents, content that is a single screen (use presentation: 'modal' if it needs its own navigation), a drag affordance beyond sheetGrabberVisible, and explicitly sized content for sheetAllowedDetents: 'fitToContents'.
standards.why: Android caps detents at three and silently truncates longer lists, cannot host native headers or nested stacks in a form sheet, and shows no grabber; a flex: 1 root has no intrinsic height to fit.

values.fit: sheetAllowedDetents: 'fitToContents' needs explicit size, not flex: 1

standards.title: Safari theme bar must match the overlay
standards.rule: Sync Safari's theme-color with a drawer overlay only if it stays in step with the overlay: precompute the opaque color the overlay makes over the background, interpolate to it along the drawer's own curve when the drawer opens, pick the color from a linear interpolation by drag progress while dragging, and leave the sync out if it falls out of step.
standards.why: Linear interpolation will not match a drawer on a custom bezier curve, and the author has not shipped the theme-bar sync in Vaul because it does not match the overlay transition when frames drop.

standards.title: Feedback on press, commit on release
standards.rule: Show press feedback the instant the pointer or finger goes down (:active, or pointerdown / onPressIn when JavaScript is needed) and commit the action on release; never show feedback only on click.
standards.why: Waiting for click or touch-up to show anything feels dead and reads as lag even at 0ms, because the finger has already left.

standards.title: Hold to confirm: slow press, fast release
standards.rule: When a destructive action that a plain click fires too easily uses hold-to-confirm, make the press slow and the release fast: an overlay clipped to inset(0 100% 0 0) fills to inset(0 0 0 0) over 2s linear while pressed and snaps back over 200ms ease-out on release, with scale(0.97) on the button.
standards.why: Be slow where the person is deciding and snappy where the system responds (symmetric timing on a hold is a review finding); linear is right because the fill is a progress indicator.

standards.title: Dismiss toasts from code by id
standards.rule: Remove a toast from code with toast.dismiss(id), using the id that toast() returns (or t.id inside toast.custom), and call toast.dismiss() with no id only when every visible toast should go.
standards.why: toast.dismiss(id) is the documented way to remove a toast programmatically; called without an id it dismisses all toasts at once.

values.one: const id = toast('Event has been created'); toast.dismiss(id);
values.headless: toast.custom((t) => <jsx />): t gives the id to dismiss

standards.title: Detect touch by capability, never by device
standards.rule: Decide touch behavior with media queries and platform features ((hover), (pointer), env(), dvh), written for touch and mouse at the same time; never branch on user-agent strings or screen width to guess at touch, and never reach for a JavaScript touch-detection hook where a media query does it.
standards.why: Touch and mouse are not exclusive (iPads with trackpads, laptops with touchscreens, phones with a mouse), and almost every mobile fix is one CSS declaration or meta tag, so a useIsTouchDevice() hook to hide hover states is the wrong tool.

review.message: Detect touch with (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) media queries, not the user agent or a touch-detection hook.

standards.title: Remove the tap highlight flash globally
standards.rule: Set html { -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent; } once, globally, and give every tappable element its own :active state in the same change.
standards.why: The translucent flash iOS Safari and Android Chrome paint over a tapped element is the loudest 'this is a website' signal and fights the designed press feedback; removing it removes the only feedback the browser gave, so :active has to replace it.

review.message: Set -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent and give the element its own :active state.

standards.title: Press feedback scales to 0.97, briefly
standards.rule: Scale every pressable element to 0.97 while it is pressed (:active on the web; keep it within 0.95–0.98), scaling the whole element so its label and icons come along, with a transform transition of 100–160ms ease-out on the web and 100–150ms in React Native (Pressable plus a Reanimated CSS transition, with 120ms and a 3% scale as the ceiling), using the codebase's existing ease-out curve rather than a new one.
standards.why: Scale takes the label and icons with it, so the press reads as physical and confirms the interface heard the user; the React Native recipe treats 120ms and a 3% scale as the ceiling for something touched this often.

values.easing: ease-out (var(--ease-out); don't fork a new curve)
values.web-sample: transition: transform 100ms var(--ease-out), background 100ms; .button:active { transform: scale(0.97); background: var(--gray-4); }
values.react-native-recipe: transitionProperty: 'transform', transitionDuration: '120ms', transitionTimingFunction: 'cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)', pressed: transform [{ scale: 0.97 }]
values.ceiling: 120ms and a 3% scale for something touched this often

engine.note: New token for the pressed scale of every pressable, created in every export from this mapping's number type (engine.py std_token_types).
Already 100ms (no change, tested); motion.transition.feedback uses it, and 100ms sits inside both press ranges (web 100–160ms, React Native 100–150ms) and matches the mobile-native sample

review.message: Keep press feedback subtle: scale(0.97) on :active, within 0.95–0.98.

standards.title: Remove the tap delay on tappables
standards.rule: Apply touch-action: manipulation to button, a, [role="button"] and every other tappable element.
standards.why: Browsers wait after a tap (the 300ms click delay) to see whether a double-tap zoom follows, and iOS Safari still delays on some elements even with width=device-width; manipulation says the element never double-tap-zooms, so click fires immediately.

standards.title: Add double-tap handling only where needed
standards.rule: Add double-tap detection only where a double-tap action truly exists.
standards.why: Double-tap detection unavoidably delays single taps, so only pay that cost where a double-tap does something.

standards.title: Let a drifting finger keep its press
standards.rule: Keep a press alive when the finger drifts a little (pressRetentionOffset in React Native, about 10px of hysteresis or hit padding on the web), and let the user cancel a tap by dragging away and back.
standards.why: A finger drifting a few pixels should not cancel a press the user meant.

values.web: ~10px of hysteresis/hit padding around the target

standards.title: Touch targets 44pt on iOS, 48dp on Android
standards.rule: Make every touch target at least 44×44pt on iOS and 48dp on Android, and give small controls on the web a 44px hit area for touch; when the visual is smaller, grow the hit area (hitSlop, or a pseudo-element on the web), never the visual.
standards.why: Small buttons are hard to tap; hitSlop brings a small icon up to the 44pt target without growing it.

engine.note: unchanged: OpenDesigner already sets size.target.touch (and size.target.min) to 44px at default settings

OpenDesigner's default size.target.min is already 44px; the CSS export lowers --ds-size-target-min to 24px (size.target.pointer) under @media (pointer: fine), which the source, about tapping, does not address

standards.title: Size full-height layouts with dvh and svh
standards.rule: Use height: 100dvh for app shells, drawers and bottom-pinned UI and min-height: 100svh for marketing heroes and first screens; never use 100vh or lvh for them (keep a 100vh line above only as a fallback when the support matrix needs old browsers).
standards.why: 100vh is the largest viewport, so on load it overflows by the URL bar and a bottom-pinned button sits under it; dvh tracks the visible area as the browser chrome shows and hides, while svh is stable and never cut off, and dvh on a marketing hero causes layout shifts mid-scroll.

review.message: Use height: 100dvh (h-dvh) for app shells and bottom-pinned UI and min-height: 100svh (min-h-svh) for heroes; keep 100vh only as a fallback line above them.

standards.title: Form inputs at 16px or larger
standards.rule: Set the text of input, textarea and select to at least 16px (1rem at the default root size); if the design wants smaller input text on desktop, apply the 16px only under @media (pointer: coarse).
standards.why: iOS Safari zooms the page when focus lands on an input under 16px and does not zoom back out on blur, leaving the user on a cropped, drifted layout.

engine.note: New token for the text size of inputs, textareas and selects (tested: engine.py set creates a dimension token in primitives.tokens.json); the CSS export writes font sizes in rem, so it becomes 1rem

review.message: Make input, textarea and select text at least 16px so iOS Safari does not zoom on focus.

standards.title: Open the right software keyboard per field
standards.rule: Give each field the keyboard it needs: inputmode="numeric" for codes, inputmode="decimal" for amounts, type="email" and type="tel" for those fields, autocapitalize="none" and autocorrect="off" on usernames and codes, and an enterkeyhint ("send", "search" or "done") so the return key says what it does.
standards.why: A field should open the software keyboard its content needs, and enterkeyhint makes the return key say what it does; the source sets these while fixing inputs for a phone.

standards.title: Contain overscroll in app layouts
standards.rule: In apps with their own scroll containers, a drawer the user drags down, or a canvas, set overscroll-behavior: none on html and body and overflow-y: auto with overscroll-behavior: contain on every inner scrollable; keep the page's default overscroll only for a scrolling document where pull-to-refresh is welcome.
standards.why: Scrolling past the top triggers pull-to-refresh on Android Chrome and the whole-page rubber band on iOS, which is wrong in an app; contain keeps a container's own native-feeling bounce but stops scroll from chaining to the page behind it.

standards.title: Never stop overscroll with touchmove listeners
standards.rule: Never stop overscroll or pull-to-refresh with a touchmove listener that calls preventDefault(); use overscroll-behavior instead.
standards.why: The listener blocks scrolling entirely and makes the listener non-passive, which costs frames.

review.message: Use overscroll-behavior (none on the root, contain on inner scrollers) instead of preventDefault on touchmove.

standards.title: Paint edge to edge, pad the safe areas
standards.rule: Add viewport-fit=cover to the viewport meta tag and pad fixed headers, bottom tab bars, toasts and sheets with env(safe-area-inset-*), with a 0px fallback when the inset is used in calc(); in React Native, offset floating UI such as toasts by the safe-area insets.
standards.why: Native apps paint edge to edge and pad their content away from the notch, Dynamic Island and home indicator; without viewport-fit=cover every env() inset is 0px, and a toast at bottom: 16 sits under the home indicator on every modern iPhone.

standards.title: Make controls unselectable, keep content selectable
standards.rule: Set user-select: none, -webkit-user-select: none and -webkit-touch-callout: none on controls (button, [role="button"], tabs, chips, drag handles) and never on body or on text that is content.
standards.why: Holding a finger on a web button selects its label or pops the copy/share callout, which native controls never do, while users copy addresses, error messages and order numbers from content; the same declaration is correct on a button and a defect on body text.

review.message: Keep content selectable: put user-select: none only on controls.

standards.title: Set touch-action per gesture surface
standards.rule: On custom gesture surfaces set touch-action to what the browser may still do: pan-y on a horizontal JavaScript carousel, pan-x on a vertical sheet handle, and none only on a surface whose gesture owns every axis (a drag-to-dismiss sheet, a slider), never on something the user must scroll past.
standards.why: A horizontal swipe is ambiguous to the browser, which often jitters the page up while the carousel moves; none means the element handles everything, so elsewhere the user cannot scroll past it.

review.message: Never put touch-action: none on the page; use it only on a surface whose gesture owns every axis, and pan-x or pan-y elsewhere.

standards.title: Prefer native scroll-snap carousels
standards.rule: When a carousel can be native scroll, build it with scroll-snap-type: x mandatory on the track and scroll-snap-align: start on the slides instead of a JavaScript gesture.
standards.why: The browser's own physics beat a hand-rolled spring, and touch-action becomes unnecessary.

standards.title: One theme-color per color scheme
standards.rule: Ship one theme-color meta tag per prefers-color-scheme plus <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">, valued at the color at the very top of the page (the header background, not the brand color); update it from JavaScript when the theme switches by class, and make an installed PWA's status-bar style and manifest colors the same decision.
standards.why: The status bar and browser chrome take their color from theme-color, so a single value gives light mode a dark bar or dark mode a white one.

review.message: Give each prefers-color-scheme its own theme-color, set to the header background.

standards.title: Ship the mobile baseline first
standards.rule: Before the first component of a mobile-facing web app, ship the baseline: the viewport meta with width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover and interactive-widget=resizes-content; one theme-color per scheme; html with -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent, -webkit-text-size-adjust: 100% and overscroll-behavior: none; 16px inputs; touch-action: manipulation and user-select: none on button, a and [role="button"]; and every :hover rule inside @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine).
standards.why: It is the floor for feeling native on mobile; interactive-widget=resizes-content makes the software keyboard shrink the layout viewport on Android Chrome so 100dvh and bottom-pinned inputs react as they do on iOS, and -webkit-text-size-adjust: 100% prevents font inflation in landscape.

values.controls: button, a, [role="button"] { touch-action: manipulation; user-select: none; -webkit-user-select: none; }

standards.title: Report mobile fixes in a few lines
standards.rule: After mobile work, report in a few lines what was wrong (the symptom and a one-line why), what changed (file and declaration) and what still needs a phone or an on-device feel check, without padding it into a report.
standards.why: The code is the deliverable, and gestures, velocity handoff and haptic timing cannot be judged from code.

standards.title: Ignore extra fingers during a drag
standards.rule: Once a drag starts, ignore every additional touch point until the user releases (for example, return early from the press handler while isDragging is true).
standards.why: Otherwise adding or switching a finger mid-drag makes the element jump to the new position, and the drawer feels off.

standards.title: Redesign hover affordances for touch
standards.rule: In a mobile app, move every affordance the web puts in hover into press, position or nothing, redesigning it rather than porting it.
standards.why: There is no hover on mobile.

standards.title: Use Gesture Handler, never PanResponder
standards.rule: Build gestures with react-native-gesture-handler (Gesture.Pan()), never PanResponder.
standards.why: PanResponder is one of the source's examples of animating on the wrong thread, which drops to 20fps on a three-year-old Android; the Never Ship table replaces it with Gesture.Pan().

review.message: Use Gesture.Pan() from react-native-gesture-handler.

standards.title: Use scheduleOnRN, not runOnJS
standards.rule: Call back to the React Native runtime from a worklet with scheduleOnRN(fn, ...args) from react-native-worklets, not the deprecated runOnJS(fn)(...args).
standards.why: runOnJS is deprecated in Reanimated 4 and scheduleOnRN replaces it.

review.message: Use scheduleOnRN(fn, ...args) from react-native-worklets.

standards.title: Cross to the JS thread only at thresholds
standards.rule: Never schedule a React Native runtime call inside onUpdate or a scroll handler; make it in onEnd, or in a useAnimatedReaction that fires once when a value crosses a threshold (a detent, a snap, pull-to-refresh arming).
standards.why: Inside onUpdate the call is queued 60–120 times a second; with useAnimatedReaction the comparison runs on the UI thread every frame and the JS call happens only when the state flips.

values.never: scheduleOnRN in onUpdate or a scroll handler (60–120× per second)
values.instead: onEnd, or useAnimatedReaction at a threshold

standards.title: Touch shared values only outside render
standards.rule: Read and write shared values only in worklets, handlers and effects, with .get() and .set() (functional form sv.set((v) => v + 1)); never during render and never through .value.
standards.why: A read during render is a snapshot that never updates and silently desyncs, a write fires mid-reconciliation and is replayed by re-renders you did not cause, and .value is the form the React Compiler cannot see through.

standards.title: Mark worklet helpers with 'worklet'
standards.rule: Put 'worklet' as the first line of every function called from a worklet.
standards.why: Without it the function throws at runtime on device while working fine in the debugger.

standards.title: Set up Reanimated so motion runs
standards.rule: Install motion packages with npx expo install, wrap the app once in GestureHandlerRootView (style { flex: 1 }, in the Expo Router root _layout), add KeyboardProvider there when react-native-keyboard-controller is used, and run Reanimated 4 on the New Architecture.
standards.why: npx expo install resolves the versions that match the project's SDK; without GestureHandlerRootView gestures do nothing with no error, keyboard hooks do nothing without the provider, Reanimated 4 requires the New Architecture, and a missing or misplaced worklets Babel plugin throws 'Failed to create a worklet'.

values.install: npx expo install react-native-reanimated react-native-worklets react-native-gesture-handler expo-haptics
values.keyboard: KeyboardProvider in the root _layout, next to GestureHandlerRootView
values.babel: babel-preset-expo configures the worklets plugin; a bare React Native project adds it manually, last in the list

standards.title: Unlock 120fps on ProMotion iPhones
standards.rule: Confirm that expo.ios.infoPlist sets CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone to true, and add it if it is missing.
standards.why: On ProMotion iPhones third-party animations are capped at 60fps unless it is set; with it the frame budget is 8ms, not 16.

review.message: Set CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone to true so animations can run at 120fps.

standards.title: Use native pieces instead of JS rebuilds
standards.rule: Use the platform's own pieces instead of rebuilding them in JavaScript: presentation: 'formSheet' for a bottom sheet that is its own screen, NativeTabs for the tab bar, Link.Menu and Link.Preview for context menus and press-and-hold previews, headerLargeTitleEnabled for a header that collapses into a large title, RefreshControl for pull to refresh, and ReanimatedSwipeable for rows that reveal actions.
standards.why: These are the platform's real components with their behaviors and transitions included (formSheet is a real UISheetPresentationController, free and correct); build a custom sheet only when it has to live inside an existing screen, and a custom refresh or swipe only when it is a signature interaction or different in kind.

review.message: headerLargeTitle is deprecated: use headerLargeTitleEnabled on the native stack.

standards.title: Screen transitions stay on the native stack
standards.rule: Configure screen-to-screen transitions with Expo Router native stack options at the platform's default duration, never rebuilt in JavaScript: animation: 'default' going deeper into a hierarchy, presentation: 'modal' for a self-contained task the user can abandon, and presentation: 'formSheet' with detents for a short interruption such as a picker, filter or share.
standards.why: The native transition runs on the platform side, keeps the interactive back gesture and matches every other app on the device; navigation matches the platform (iOS push is 350ms) even though UI motion beats it.

standards.title: Back swipe mirrors custom transitions
standards.rule: Set animationMatchesGesture: true on every screen that sets a custom animation.
standards.why: It makes the iOS back swipe run the transition in reverse under the finger; otherwise dragging back looks like a different app than pushing forward.

standards.title: Translate before scale in transform arrays
standards.rule: Put translate before scale in a React Native transform array ([{ translateY }, { scale }]) unless you want the translate multiplied.
standards.why: transform is an array and order matters: reversed, the translate gets scaled too.

standards.title: Reanimated springs use duration and dampingRatio
standards.rule: Configure Reanimated springs with duration and dampingRatio from the source's table, never mass, stiffness and damping: { duration: 400, dampingRatio: 1 } for a default settle, { duration: 400, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity } to reposition or snap back after a drag, { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity } for sheets and drawers, plus overshootClamping: true wherever motion must not pass a hard edge; allow overshoot only when the gesture carried momentum.
standards.why: Reanimated's spring takes Apple's two designer parameters directly and values must not be approximated; overshoot feels right on a card you flicked and wrong on a menu that faded in, and a dismissed sheet without overshootClamping springs past the bottom and flashes a gap.

values.sheet-dismiss-recipe: withSpring(HEIGHT, { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 1, velocity: e.velocityY, overshootClamping: true })

engine.note: The default settle has no overshoot (dampingRatio 1); the 0.8 configs belong to momentum-carrying gestures, which have no token, so they stay in code (tested: engine.py set accepts it and changes the three spatial springs) [inferred]

standards.title: Clamp every scroll-driven interpolation
standards.rule: Drive scroll-linked motion from useAnimatedScrollHandler into a shared value (scrollEventThrottle={16}) and pass Extrapolation.CLAMP to every scroll-driven interpolate.
standards.why: Without CLAMP, scrolling past the input range keeps driving the output, so a header's opacity goes negative and it reappears inverted at the bottom of a long list.

standards.title: Follow the keyboard frame by frame
standards.rule: Move keyboard-following UI with react-native-keyboard-controller's useReanimatedKeyboardAnimation (translateY from its height, 0 to -keyboardHeight, on the UI thread), never with Keyboard.addListener plus a timing animation.
standards.why: The keyboard rides a private system curve and the event reaches the JS thread after the keyboard has started moving, so any duration visibly lags or leads it.

review.message: If this moves UI with the keyboard, use useReanimatedKeyboardAnimation from react-native-keyboard-controller.

standards.title: Map haptics to the moment
standards.rule: Pick the expo-haptics call by moment: Haptics.selectionAsync() when a value ticks past a step (picker, slider detent, segmented control, tab press), impactAsync(Light) when something snaps home, a sheet detent catches, a drag commits or a pull crosses its refresh threshold, impactAsync(Medium) when a heavy object lands or a destructive action fires, and notificationAsync(Success or Error) when an operation succeeds or fails.
standards.why: Used sparingly, haptics make the app feel expensive; used everywhere, users turn them off.

standards.title: Same press scale on iOS and Android
standards.rule: Use the Android ripple only in a Material-styled app; in a custom-designed app give both platforms the same press scale.
standards.why: The same scale on both platforms is more coherent than a ripple on one.

standards.title: Apply each mobile fix where its reason applies
standards.rule: Ship every mobile fix with its reason and apply it only where that reason applies, not globally out of habit: user-select: none belongs on a button, never on body text.
standards.why: Each fix has a why, and the same declaration is correct in one place and a defect in another; user-select: none on body text is a defect, on a button it is correct.

values.example: user-select: none on controls only, never on body

standards.title: Cap body text near 65ch
standards.rule: Cap the width of body text at about 65ch instead of letting it stretch the full width of its container.
standards.why: Line length stays comfortable to read.

standards.title: Tabular digits for changing numbers
standards.rule: Apply font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums to price columns and to numbers that change in place, such as tickers, timers and counters.
standards.why: Fixed-width digits line up so a price column reads cleanly, and changing numbers do not shift around as they update.

standards.title: Use the ellipsis character
standards.rule: Write the single ellipsis character (…) in markup and UI strings, never three periods (...).
standards.why: Truncation then follows the container instead of snapping at a fixed character count.

review.message: Three periods in UI text: use the ellipsis character … instead.

standards.title: Loosen tracking on uppercase labels
standards.rule: Give uppercase labels looser letter-spacing than the same text in sentence case.
standards.why: Tight uppercase reads cramped.

standards.title: Make letter-spacing specific to size
standards.rule: Never use one letter-spacing value for every size: tighten large display text and headings (for example letter-spacing: -0.02em), give small text slightly positive tracking, and leave body text near 0.
standards.why: Letters read too far apart as text grows, and small text needs slightly positive tracking for legibility, so a fixed letter-spacing is wrong somewhere.

standards.title: Leading tracks size inversely
standards.rule: Set line-height inversely to size: tight on large headings (for example 1.05 for display text), looser on body copy (for example 1.5), higher for scripts with tall ascenders and descenders, and tighter for dense, information-heavy UI.
standards.why: Type should change shape with size, as Apple designs it; the source gives no further reason for the example values.

standards.title: Build hierarchy from weight, size, leading
standards.rule: Build type hierarchy from weight, size and line-height set together, not from font size alone.
standards.why: The source states the set as the rule and adds that weight gives presence without taking more space.

standards.title: Emphasise with weight, not italic
standards.rule: Emphasise interface text with weight (bold); keep italic for citations and linguistic stress in prose.
standards.why: Italic hierarchy reads like print editorial, not UI hierarchy, while weight adds presence without taking more space.

standards.title: Reserve underlines for links
standards.rule: Underline only links; emphasise non-link text with weight or color, never with an underline.
standards.why: Underline stays a reliable affordance, and people are not tempted to click inert copy.

review.message: Underline on text that is not a link: emphasise with weight or color instead.

standards.title: Metric-matched fallback font stack
standards.rule: Declare a fallback font stack whose x-height and weight match the primary typeface.
standards.why: Font loading then does not cause layout shift.

standards.title: Default to the system font
standards.rule: Start from the platform's system font and switch to a custom typeface only for a stated reason.
standards.why: The system font already ships optical sizing, tracking tables and legibility tuning.

standards.title: Legible text on translucent surfaces
standards.rule: Over blurred or translucent surfaces, avoid flat gray text: use higher-contrast text, a slightly heavier weight and a small letter-spacing increase.
standards.why: Vibrancy keeps text legible over changing backgrounds.

standards.title: Semi-transparent shadow over solid border
standards.rule: Separate surfaces with a semi-transparent shadow rather than a solid, opaque border.
standards.why: A solid border where a semi-transparent shadow belongs is one of the small agent mistakes that compound into an interface that is not great.

standards.title: Scroll-edge effects, not hard dividers
standards.rule: Instead of a 1px border under a sticky header, fade a small blur or gradient mask where content meets floating chrome, and only where floating UI actually overlaps content.
standards.why: The source prefers a soft edge that appears only where floating chrome overlaps content over a permanent hard divider; it gives no further reason.

review.message: 1px divider under a sticky header: fade a scroll-edge blur or gradient mask where content passes under it.

standards.title: Translucent bars and sheets
standards.rule: Build navigation bars, toolbars and sheets as translucent layers (backdrop-filter: blur() over a semi-transparent background) with content scrolling underneath, not as opaque bars that take a fixed strip.
standards.why: Translucent materials bring structure as a floating functional layer without stealing focus.

standards.title: Material weight encodes hierarchy
standards.rule: Use darker, heavier materials to separate structural regions such as sidebars, and lighter materials to draw attention to interactive elements such as buttons.
standards.why: Material weight encodes hierarchy.

standards.title: Never stack light translucent surfaces
standards.rule: Never place a light translucent surface on top of another light translucent surface.
standards.why: Legibility collapses when light translucent layers stack.

standards.title: Bigger surfaces read thicker
standards.rule: Give bigger surfaces a stronger blur and a deeper shadow than small chips.
standards.why: Bigger surfaces should read as thicker material.

standards.title: Scrim for modal tasks only
standards.rule: Pair a modal task's surface with a dimming scrim and push the background back or down; give a parallel, non-blocking panel translucency and offset without a scrim; in a stack of sheets, progressively dim and push back each parent layer.
standards.why: Dimming focuses a modal task, while separating without a scrim keeps a parallel flow unbroken.

standards.title: Color on solid layers
standards.rule: Put color on a solid layer, not on a translucent foreground surface.
standards.why: The source puts it with vibrancy, which keeps text legible over changing backgrounds; it gives no separate reason.

standards.title: Colors adapt to light and dark
standards.rule: Make interface colors adapt to light and dark mode: give each color role a light value and a dark value.
standards.why: The source lists colors that adapt to light and dark as part of the craft that builds trust.

standards.title: Restrained look with no project
standards.rule: When prototyping with no project to draw tokens from (an empty directory, or the person is just exploring), use a restrained default look: neutral grays, one accent color and the system font stack.
standards.why: The source gives no reason; with no project there are no tokens for the variants to use [inferred].

standards.title: Use and extend existing tokens
standards.rule: Build UI from the project's existing tokens (colors, radii, spacing, fonts, easing and duration variables) and extend them when something is missing; never add a parallel set, and never hand-type or approximate a value such as cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1).
standards.why: Every variant should look like it could ship in the product tomorrow, and a parallel token system is a defect.

review.message: Hand-typed cubic-bezier in a transition: use the motion.easing token (its CSS variable) instead.

standards.title: Make every value a deliberate choice
standards.rule: Make every spacing, timing and alignment value a deliberate choice you can defend.
standards.why: Uncompromising attention to detail builds trust.

standards.title: No jitter, misalignment or rotation breaks
standards.rule: Do not ship jittery scrolling, misaligned icons or layouts that break when the device rotates.
standards.why: These read as carelessness.

standards.title: Hierarchy makes the key thing obvious
standards.rule: Use order, spacing and contrast so the most important thing on a screen is the most obvious.
standards.why: Clarity through hierarchy is part of simplicity.

standards.title: Aim for simplicity, not minimalism
standards.rule: Strip what is unnecessary so the core purpose shows, make every element earn its place, and add context where it simplifies; do not bury everything in one place to look minimal.
standards.why: Burying everything in one place looks minimal but is not simple; sometimes adding context simplifies (a video scrubber that shows time remaining).

standards.title: Show the common path first
standards.rule: Show the common path first and put advanced options one level deeper.
standards.why: The source lists this under simplicity.

standards.title: Controls sit near what they change
standards.rule: Place each control near what it affects and arrange controls to mirror what they change.
standards.why: Proximity implies relationship; if a control needs a label to explain it, the mapping is weak.

standards.title: Every screen answers wayfinding
standards.rule: Never trap the user: every screen should answer Where am I? Where can I go? What's there? How do I get out?
standards.why: The source lists wayfinding as a tactical rule serving the design principles.

standards.title: Name navigation items for their contents
standards.rule: Name navigation items for their contents (for example "Progress", "Library"), not with vague umbrellas such as "Home".
standards.why: Specificity creates predictability.

standards.title: Keep interface copy plain and concise
standards.rule: Keep interface copy concise: plain language, no jargon and fewer steps.
standards.why: The source lists conciseness under simplicity.

standards.title: Same look, same behaviour
standards.rule: Make things that look the same behave the same and live in the same place.
standards.why: People can then predict what happens next (close is always top-left on macOS).

standards.title: Break familiar patterns only with proof
standards.rule: Break a familiar pattern only when you can prove the new one is better, and test it rather than assume.
standards.why: Familiarity lets people build on what they already know.

standards.title: Metaphors with honest physics
standards.rule: Use metaphors that are neither too literal nor too abstract (a trash can means delete) and honour their physics.
standards.why: The source lists this under familiarity: building on what people already know.

standards.title: Offer choices, not one forced path
standards.rule: Keep people in control by offering choices instead of forcing a single path.
standards.why: The source names this agency.

standards.title: Undo for slips, confirm only destruction
standards.rule: Give easy undo for slips, and use a confirmation dialog only for genuinely destructive, irreversible actions, sparingly.
standards.why: Overusing confirmation dialogs trains people to click through them.

standards.title: Ask for private data carefully
standards.rule: Ask for private data at the moment it is needed, only for what is needed, and say why.
standards.why: The source names this responsibility: acting in the user's interest.

standards.title: Adapt to platform and situation
standards.rule: Adapt the design to the platform and situation: quick touch interactions on a phone, deep workflows with precise pointer control on desktop.
standards.why: The source names this flexibility: designing for different contexts and devices.

standards.title: Design for every age and ability
standards.rule: Design for the full range of age, language, expertise and ability.
standards.why: The source names this flexibility: designing for the full range of abilities.

standards.title: Decide what not to build
standards.rule: Decide what not to build, and spend the user's time, attention and trust only on features that pay off.
standards.why: Every feature asks for the user's time, attention and trust.

standards.title: Anticipate misuse and harm
standards.rule: Anticipate misuse and harm, especially in AI features: add previews, confirmations and disclaimers, and cut a feature whose risk outweighs its value.
standards.why: The source names this responsibility: acting in the user's interest (an allergy-aware recipe app must not suggest a harmful ingredient).

standards.title: Keep evolving the design
standards.rule: Keep evolving the design as features and hardware change.
standards.why: Craft needs iteration and longevity.

standards.title: Decide the emotion, then reinforce it
standards.rule: Decide the emotion people should feel (for example calm, confident or excited) and reinforce it in every decision instead of tacking delight on top.
standards.why: Delight is the result of getting the other seven principles right, not confetti tacked on top.

standards.title: Reason with the eight principles
standards.rule: Name Apple's eight principles (purpose, agency, responsibility, familiarity, flexibility, simplicity, craft, delight) when making and defending design decisions.
standards.why: The source says to use them as the names you reason with.

values.principles: purpose, agency, responsibility, familiarity, flexibility, simplicity, craft, delight

standards.title: Feedback on every action
standards.rule: Give feedback as soon as possible: confirm meaningful actions (a loading state while a submitted form works, a success state after copy to clipboard), expose ongoing status, warn before problems, and validate form input inline rather than on submit.
standards.why: The interface should feel as if it is listening to the user.

standards.title: Polish the unseen details
standards.rule: Build the small details users will not consciously notice, such as matching the behaviour people expect from native components.
standards.why: In the aggregate, unseen details become visible and compound; when a feature works exactly as someone assumes, they carry on without a second thought.

standards.title: Excellent defaults before options
standards.rule: Make the default easing, timing and visual design of a component excellent before adding options.
standards.why: Most users never customize, so a component should ship beautiful out of the box.

standards.title: Pick libraries from the curated list
standards.rule: When a frontend task needs a library, identify the task rather than the library the person named, and recommend one library from the curated list in one sentence, not a menu of options when the list has a clear answer; do not substitute an alternative from outside the list unless the person asks for one, say explicitly when a task is not covered before recommending from general knowledge, and never install an abandoned package.
standards.why: The picks are deliberate and taste-driven; the list exists so an agent picks the right library instead of hand-rolling a component or installing an abandoned package.

standards.title: Reuse installed libraries first
standards.rule: Read package.json before recommending a library: use a listed library the project already has, and when it uses a competitor (for example react-window instead of Virtuoso), flag the recommendation without replacing the dependency unless asked.
standards.why: The source says not to churn a working dependency without being asked; it gives no further reason.

standards.title: Never hand-roll standard components
standards.rule: When a task needs a component rather than an animation (a toast, a drawer, a command menu, a dropdown), pick a library instead of hand-rolling it; build toasts with Sonner, never by hand or with a modal library.
standards.why: Hand-rolling these is how you end up with a <div> dropdown and no focus management; for toasts, Sonner exists for exactly this.

standards.title: Animate numbers with NumberFlow
standards.rule: When a number animates (a counter, price or stat), use NumberFlow instead of animating it by re-rendering the text.
standards.why: NumberFlow handles digit transitions properly.

standards.title: Shared state in zustand
standards.rule: Keep shared state in zustand instead of a useState-per-component web of props.
standards.why: The source lists a useState-per-component web of props for shared state as a mismatch.

standards.title: clsx or cva for conditional classes
standards.rule: Build conditional className strings with clsx, or with cva when the component has real variants (size, intent, state); never nest template-literal ternaries three conditions deep.
standards.why: clsx is for ad-hoc conditional classes and cva for variants that deserve a typed API; they compose.

review.message: Three or more ternaries in a template-literal className: use clsx, or cva for variants.

standards.title: Let people personalise when one layout can't fit
standards.rule: When no single layout fits everyone, let people personalise it: rearrange controls and hide what they don't use.
standards.why: The source lists this under flexibility: designing for different contexts, devices and the full range of abilities.

standards.title: Motion that merely runs is not done
standards.rule: Never ship motion, AI-written or not, just because it runs: treat a transition that works but feels sluggish, lands from the wrong origin, fires too often or drops frames as a regression, and keep flagging it until it meets every approval criterion.
standards.why: AI produces motion that works but feels mediocre, and if you can't tell the difference you'll ship it and settle for good enough, which is not good enough. The review bias is toward motion that feels right, not motion that merely runs: approval is earned, not assumed.

standards.title: Review motion against the full craft bar
standards.rule: Review every animation in a change against all ten review standards and flag every escalation trigger on sight; a violation of any standard is a finding.
standards.why: Every animation in the diff is measured against the ten non-negotiable standards and a violation is a finding; the escalation triggers are flagged on sight, hard, because the review is meant to be strict.

values.ten-standards: justified motion; frequency-appropriate; responsive easing; sub-300ms UI; origin & physical correctness; interruptibility; GPU-only properties; accessibility; asymmetric enter/exit; cohesion
values.flag-on-sight: transition: all; scale(0) or pure-fade entrances with no initial transform; ease-in on any UI interaction or weak built-in easing on a deliberate animation; animation on a keyboard shortcut, command-palette toggle or 100+/day action; UI duration > 300ms with no stated reason; transform-origin: center on a trigger-anchored popover/dropdown/tooltip; keyframes on toasts, toggles or anything added/triggered rapidly; animating width/height/margin/padding/top/left; Framer Motion x/y/scale props on motion that runs while the page is busy; updating a CSS variable on a parent to drive a child transform; missing prefers-reduced-motion handling on movement; ungated :hover motion; symmetric enter/exit timing on a press-and-release or hold interaction; everything-at-once entrance where a 30–80ms stagger belongs

standards.title: Self-check motion before finishing
standards.rule: Before you finish an animation, self-check it against the animate Never Ship list, and before you finish a mobile web change, against the mobile-native Never Ship list; build motion so it passes a strict review the first time.
standards.why: Each item on the animate Never Ship list is an automatic block in review-animations, and the construction bar is the same bar that review enforces; the mobile-native list is the self-check for the tells that make a web app feel like a website on a phone.

values.never-ship-motion: transition: all; transform: scale(0) entrance; ease-in on a UI element; built-in ease-out on a deliberate animation; animation on a keyboard shortcut or 100+/day action; UI duration over 300ms with no reason; transform-origin: center on a trigger-anchored popover; keyframes on toasts, toggles, rapidly-triggered elements; animating width/height/margin/padding/top/left; Motion x/y/scale props under load; ungated :hover motion; missing prefers-reduced-motion; everything entering at once
values.never-ship-mobile-web: user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1 (fix: 16px inputs); ungated :hover; 100vh for an app shell or bottom-pinned UI (use 100dvh); 100dvh on a marketing hero (use 100svh); press feedback on click only (use :active / pointerdown); touchmove + preventDefault() to stop overscroll (use overscroll-behavior); user-select: none on body (only on controls); touch-action: none on something the user needs to scroll past (use pan-x / pan-y); env(safe-area-inset-*) without viewport-fit=cover; one theme-color for both schemes; user-agent sniffing to detect touch; declaring it fixed from device emulation

standards.title: Report review findings as one table
standards.rule: Report motion and UI review findings as a single markdown table with Before, After and Why columns, one row per issue, never as a list of separate 'Before:' and 'After:' lines.
standards.why: Both review skills mark this format as required and show the line-by-line format as wrong; the Why column briefly explains the reasoning for each change.

values.never: a Before:/After: list on separate lines

standards.title: Close every motion review with Block or Approve
standards.rule: After the findings table, group the remaining review commentary by impact tier, highest first, omitting empty tiers, and end every motion review with an explicit Block or Approve decision under the stated criteria.
standards.why: The verdict is a required part of the review output and must close with an explicit decision; approval is earned only when every approval criterion is met.

values.tiers: 1 Feel-breaking regressions; 2 Missed simplifications; 3 Performance; 4 Interruptibility & timing; 5 Origin, physicality & cohesion; 6 Accessibility
values.block: any feel-breaking regression, animation on a keyboard/high-frequency action, scale(0)/ease-in on UI, or a non-GPU animation with an easy GPU fix
values.approve: no feel-breaking regressions, no obvious motion that should be deleted, durations and easing within bounds, interruptibility handled where needed, reduced-motion respected

standards.title: Fix motion in the remedial order
standards.rule: When proposing fixes for motion, prefer earlier moves over later ones in the remedial hierarchy, starting with deleting the animation, and reach for blur only after other easings and durations still leave it feeling off.
standards.why: The review ranks fixes: deletion is the strongest move for high-frequency, purposeless or keyboard-triggered motion, and when unsure whether motion feels right the strongest move is often to delete it; blur is the fallback when easing and duration changes have not fixed the feel.

values.order: 1 Delete the animation (high-frequency / no purpose / keyboard-triggered); 2 Reduce it (shorter duration, smaller transform, fewer animated properties); 3 Fix the easing; 4 Fix the origin/physicality; 5 Make it interruptible; 6 Move it to the GPU; 7 Asymmetric timing; 8 Polish (blur to mask crossfades, stagger for groups, @starting-style for entry, spring for 'alive' elements); 9 Accessibility & cohesion

standards.title: Confirm and cite every finding
standards.rule: Re-read the cited code for every motion finding yourself, cite it as file:line, and drop any finding that is by design, mis-attributed, duplicated or exempt before you present it.
standards.why: Never present a finding you haven't confirmed at its file:line; some flags are correct or acceptable, such as transform-origin: center on a modal or a long duration on a marketing page.

values.exempt-examples: transform-origin: center on a modal; a long duration on a marketing page

standards.title: Spell out exact values, never vague ones
standards.rule: In every review finding, opportunity and plan, give the exact curve, duration, spring config and properties copied from the reference, never an approximation or a vague target such as 'use a nicer easing'.
standards.why: The reference holds the precise values behind the review; the person or agent acting on the finding has no taste of their own to fill in a vague target.

values.never: "use a nicer easing"; values approximated from memory

standards.title: Rank motion findings by leverage
standards.rule: Order audit findings and motion suggestions by leverage (impact ÷ effort), present audit findings as one table, and prefer a short list of high-confidence items to a long padded one, saying 'the motion here is already right' when that is true.
standards.why: The job is to find the animation work with the highest leverage, not what would be fun to build; a short list of high-confidence, high-leverage plans beats a long padded one.

values.order: leverage (impact ÷ effort), not how fun they'd be to build
values.audit-table: | # | Severity | Category | Location | Finding | Fix summary |
values.valid-result: the motion here is already right

standards.title: Rate findings HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW
standards.rule: Give every motion finding and plan exactly one severity, HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW, by the stated definitions, and let the frequency map drive it.
standards.why: The severity definitions separate feel-breaking problems from noticeably-off ones and polish, and how often an element is hit decides how much its motion matters.

values.HIGH: feel-breaking: wrong easing on UI, animation on keyboard/high-frequency actions, dropped frames, scale(0)
values.MEDIUM: noticeably off: wrong origin, non-interruptible dynamic UI, missing reduced-motion
values.LOW: polish: stagger, blur-masked crossfades, token consolidation
values.frequency-map: 100+ times/day vs occasionally vs rarely; this drives severity

standards.title: Recon before judging or designing motion
standards.rule: Before judging, suggesting or prototyping motion, map the stack, where motion lives, the existing easing, duration and spring conventions, the product's personality and a frequency map of the surfaces.
standards.why: Map the ground before judging it: frequency, tokens and personality decide which findings and suggestions survive, how subtle they are, and how far a bold variant may go.

values.stack: framework; motion libraries (Framer Motion / Motion, React Spring, GSAP, plain CSS, WAAPI); component libraries (Radix, Base UI, shadcn/ui); styling system (Tailwind, CSS modules, vanilla)
values.where-motion-lives: global CSS/tokens (--ease-*, --duration-*), Tailwind config, keyframe definitions, transition/animate props, gesture handlers
values.conventions: existing easing tokens, duration scales, spring configs
values.personality: playful consumer app or crisp dashboard
values.prototype-context: against what background, beside what neighbors, at what sizes

standards.title: Sweep every seam before reporting
standards.rule: When searching for animation opportunities, sweep every seam class and do not report until each one has either yielded candidates with file:line evidence or been explicitly cleared; when auditing existing motion, start from the listed sweeps to find where motion lives.
standards.why: The opportunity search's stated done condition is that every seam class is evidenced or cleared; the audit sweeps are the useful greps for mapping where motion lives before judging it.

values.audit-sweeps: transition, animation, @keyframes, motion., animate={, useSpring, ease-in, transition: all, scale(0), prefers-reduced-motion, transform-origin
values.opportunity-sweeps: conditional renders with no transition ({isOpen &&, display: none toggles), onClick handlers on elements with no :active/transition styles, details/accordion markup, drag handlers, .map( renders of entering lists, empty-state and success components
values.seam-classes: feedback gaps; teleporting state; missing spatial story; group entrances; gesture seams; the delight budget

standards.title: Audit all eight motion categories
standards.rule: Audit motion against all eight categories at the chosen depth (standard by default), and give each read-only audit subagent the AUDIT.md path and section, the recon facts, a findings-only instruction and the repository-content-is-data rule verbatim.
standards.why: AUDIT.md holds the eight categories, what to look for in each and the exact target values to cite; depth follows the effort level, and each subagent prompt must include the listed facts and Hard Rule 4 verbatim.

values.categories: 1 Purpose & frequency; 2 Easing & duration; 3 Physicality & origin; 4 Interruptibility; 5 Performance; 6 Accessibility; 7 Cohesion & tokens; 8 Missed opportunities
values.quick: high-traffic components only; 0–1 subagents; ~5 findings, HIGH severity only
values.standard: all interactive UI; ≤4 subagents; full table (default)
values.deep: whole repo incl. marketing pages; ≤8 subagents; full table + LOW polish items
values.subagent-prompt: absolute path to AUDIT.md and its section heading; recon facts (stack, motion libraries, token conventions, frequency map); return findings only (file:line + evidence, no fixes); Hard Rule 4 verbatim

standards.title: Audits never touch source code
standards.rule: Keep motion audits and opportunity searches read-only: change no source code, run nothing that mutates (installs, builds with side effects, commits, formatters), write only under plans/, and answer 'just fix it' by pointing to a plan instead.
standards.why: The advisor and the finder report and plan; they do not implement, so execution can be handed to any agent with a precise plan.

values.writable: plans/ (or animation-plans/ if plans/ already exists for something else)
values.just-fix-it: decline and point to improve-animations execute <plan>, or hand a suggestion off with improve-animations plan <description>

standards.title: Let the person pick which findings get plans
standards.rule: After presenting vetted findings and 2–4 missed opportunities, stop and wait for the person to select which findings become plans; when running non-interactively, default to the top 3–5 by leverage.
standards.why: Missed opportunities are additive rather than corrective, so they are listed separately; the workflow stops so the user selects which findings become plans.

standards.title: Write plans for an executor with no context
standards.rule: Write every motion fix plan so an executor with zero context and zero taste can complete it: inline exact file paths, current-code excerpts, exact target values, the repo's conventions with one exemplar file:line and ordered steps, and never refer back to earlier discussion.
standards.why: The capable model does the part where judgement compounds and hands execution to any agent, including cheaper models; the executor has no context from the conversation, so the plan must contain everything, exactly.

values.include: exact file paths and current-code excerpts; exact cubic-bezier, duration and spring values; repo conventions (token names, file placement, prop patterns) with one exemplar file:line; ordered steps; scope boundaries; verification
values.never: "use the easing discussed above"; "the audit above"; "the easing we discussed"

standards.title: Use the fixed plan template
standards.rule: Write each motion fix plan as plans/NNN-short-slug.md with the fixed header (Status TODO, Commit from git rev-parse --short HEAD, Severity, Category, Estimated scope) and the sections Problem, Target, Repo conventions to follow, Steps, Boundaries and Verification.
standards.why: Every plan written by improve-animations follows this structure because the executor may be a less capable model with zero context and zero taste; the commit stamp lets it detect drift and stop instead of improvising.

values.title: # NNN — <Short imperative title>
values.header: Status: TODO; Commit: <output of git rev-parse --short HEAD>; Severity: HIGH | MEDIUM | LOW; Category: <audit category>; Estimated scope: <n files, rough size>
values.problem: what is wrong, where, and why it matters to how the product feels; every location as path/to/file.tsx:123 with the current code verbatim
values.steps: one concrete edit per step: file, what changes, resulting code

standards.title: Plans fence the executor in
standards.rule: Give every motion plan hard boundaries: name the files it must not touch, allow motion properties only unless a step says otherwise, add no dependencies, and tell the executor to stop and report if the code has drifted from the plan.
standards.why: An executor with no taste must not improvise; drift since the commit stamp means the plan no longer matches the code.

values.boundaries: Do NOT touch <files/components out of scope>; Do NOT change markup/structure — motion properties only (unless a step says otherwise); Do NOT add new dependencies
values.on-drift: If a step doesn't match the code you find (drift since the commit stamp), STOP and report instead of improvising

standards.title: Every plan ends with a feel check
standards.rule: End every motion plan's verification with the exact mechanical commands and their expected outcome, a feel check of observable details (including 10% playback in the DevTools Animations panel and a prefers-reduced-motion toggle), and 'Done when' criteria a machine or an eye can check.
standards.why: Motion can be mechanically correct and still feel wrong, so the feel check is not optional; the executor or the person reviewing the diff needs concrete things to watch for in slow motion.

values.mechanical: exact commands (typecheck, lint, build) with expected outcome
values.feel-check: run the UI, trigger the interaction, confirm observable checks such as 'the dropdown scales from its trigger, not from center' and 'spamming the toggle never restarts the animation from zero'
values.reduced-motion: toggle prefers-reduced-motion (Rendering panel): movement dropped, opacity feedback remains

standards.title: One plan per finding, indexed
standards.rule: Write one plan per finding, merging two only when they share every file and the same fix pattern, and create or update plans/README.md with a table of plans (number, title, severity, status), the recommended execution order and the dependencies between plans.
standards.why: The plan template allows one plan per finding, merged only when two share every file and the same fix pattern; plans/README.md records the plans with their severity and status, the recommended execution order and the dependencies between plans.

values.merge-only-when: two findings share every file and the same fix pattern (e.g. the same easing token swap across components)
values.index: plans/README.md: number, title, severity, status; recommended execution order; dependencies

standards.title: Execute plans in isolation, then reconcile
standards.rule: Run a motion plan through an executor in an isolated worktree and review its diff against the review-animations bar with a verdict, and reconcile plans/ against the current code so done plans are marked DONE, stale file:line references are refreshed and fixed findings retired.
standards.why: Execution is handed to any agent but still has to pass the same strict review; plans go stale as the code moves.

values.execute <plan>: executor subagent in an isolated worktree, then review its diff with the review-animations bar and render a verdict
